title: Nitrogen-rich metal-organic framework mediated Cu–N–C composite catalysts for the electrochemical reduction of CO2
abstract: Cu-based MOFs, i.e., HKUST-1, etc., have been pertinently chosen as the pristine materials for CO2ER due to the unique ability of copper for generation hydrocarbon fuel. However, the limited conductivity and stability become the stumbling-block that prevents the development of it. The exploring of MOFs-derived M–C materials starts a new chapter for the MOFs precursors, which provides a remarkable electronic connection between carbon matrix and metals/metal oxides. N-doped M–N–C with extensive M–N sites scattering into the carbon matrix are more popular because of their impressive contribution to catalytic activity and specific product selectivity. Nevertheless, Cu–N–C system remained undeveloped up to now. The lack of ideal precursor, the sensitivity of Cu to be oxidized, and the difficulties in the synthesis of 3 / 36 small size Cu nanoparticles are thus known as the main barriers to the development of Cu–N–C electrocatalysts. Herein, a nitrogen-rich Cu–BTT MOF is employed for the derivation of N-doped Cu–N–CT composite electrocatalysts by the pyrolyze method. High-temperature pyrolysis product of Cu–N–C1100 exhibits the best catalytic activity for productions of CO (−0.6 V vs. RHE, jCO=0.4 mA/cm2) and HCOOH (−0.9 V vs. RHE, jHCOOH=1.4 mA/cm2).

sections.heading: Highlights
sections.text:
Cu–N–C electrocatalysts were prepared through the direct pyrolyze of a nitrogen-rich metal-organic framework. Well-dispersed Cu nanoparticles in 20–40 nm sizes were kept in the N-doped carbon matrix. CO (FE 40.8%) and HCOOH (FE 38.1%) were produced in high efficiencies in Cu– N–C1100. Cu–N–C1100 exhibits the highest IG/ID value, the highest contribution of pyrrolic N and NX–Cu, the highest mesoporous and microporous volume, the lowest Cu nanoparticles density in porous carbon layers, and stable CO2 capture ability.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Fossil fuels account for about four-fifths of the world's initial energy. Since the industrial society, the accelerated expenditure of fossil fuel has causing a rising level of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the atmosphere, which leads to global warming and energy crisis [1,2]. The conversion of CO2 into energy-dense fuels and chemical feedstock by employing renewable energy sources, such as solar, water, and wind power, would be a potentially attractive strategy [3]. Among the developed CO2 utilization methods, electrocatalysis is one of the most sustainable chemical routes to reduce CO2 due to its accessible reaction condition, scalable application, and tunable selectivity [4–6].
So far, various electrocatalysts have been widely employed in the field, and therefore electrochemical reduction of CO2 (CO2ER) has achieved a remarkable accomplishment. Unfortunately, in addition to the competition of hydrogen evolution reactions (HER), CO2ER technology still faces many challenges [7]. The first
4 / 36
challenge is the substantial kinetic barriers and high overpotential of CO2ER due to its low solubility and high stability in water [8]. The low selectivity of the electrode towards the required product is the second challenge since the reduction product is complex and is affected by many factors [9–10]. The catalyst deactivation is the third challenge in which the lifetime is shortened due to the adsorption of intermediates and impurities [11]. Therefore, to meet the above challenges, the exploration of alternative catalysts with high selectivity, activity, and excellent stability is an inevitable task.
Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) represents a relatively new class of hybrid porous crystalline materials composed of ordered motifs which are formed by the combination of metal ions/clusters and organic linkers [12–13]. The desirable merits, for example, structural diversity and tailorability, controllable pore size distribution, and high specific surface area make MOFs widely used in chemical sensing [14], gas capture, and separation [15], biomedicine [16], and heterogeneous catalysis [17]. Recently, MOFs-based heterogeneous electrocatalysts for CO2ER in organic or aqueous systems have been explored [18]. As is well known, Cu-based materials are the only class of catalysts reported to date that generate hydrocarbons with high selectivity and efficiency [19–21]. Thus, Cu-based MOFs become the initial entry point for CO2ER study in this subject [22–25]. As a first report, Kumar et al. employed HKUST–1 film as the catalyst for CO2ER in DMF/TBATFB solution producing a product of oxalic acid [22]. It indicates that the in situ generated Cu(I)– CO2 adduct is the active catalytic site. Shortly afterward, a Cu–rubeanate MOF (CR– MOF) catalyst was chosen for CO2ER, in which HCOOH is the only product [23]. In
5 / 36
addition to Cu-based MOFs, Zn, Co, Fe, and Re-based MOFs have also been tested [26–29]. Although the reported pristine MOFs materials show promising performance for CO2ER, however, their limited conductivity and stability inhibit the further development and utilization. To relieve these limitations, two strategies were proposed, that is the development of MOFs-based nanocomposite electrocatalysts [30–34], and the MOFs-derived carbon-based materials [35–37]. Recently, the introduction of HKUST–1 as the CO2 trapping agent into a Cu nanoparticles (NP) based gas diffusion electrode (GDE), which enhances the concentration of CO2 on the interface, was proved to be effective in the improvement of faradaic efficiency (FE) for CH4 by 2–3 fold when compares to the GDE–blank [32].
To explore the potential of HKUST–1 as the precursor for generating carbon-based hybrid materials, Quan et al. investigated the straightforward pyrolyze approach, in which the metal centers of Cu in MOFs are scattering in situ into the carbon network [35]. The remarkable electronic connection between the carbon matrix and the metals/metal oxides should account for the high FE for the alcohol products, of which a total FE is in the range of 45.2–71.2% at −0.1 V to −0.7 V vs. RHE. The MOF of ZIF–8 with plentiful pyridinic nitrogen becomes popular in the design of metal– nitrogen–carbon electrocatalysts [36–40], or nitrogen-doped carbon materials [41–42]. Many researchers have confirmed that the M–N sites scattering into the carbon matrix has impressive efficiencies for the CO2ER [43]. Besides, the CO2ER activity is much dependent on nature of the transition metal [44]. However, the pristine Zn–N sites exhibit low selectivity towards the CO2ER, as revealed by Bao et al. [38]. As a result,
6 / 36
the Zn-center in ZIF–8 was often ionic exchanged by/doped with other metals of Co, Ni, Fe, or evaporated away. Up to now, there remain undeveloped on the Cu–N–C system [44–47], probably due to the lack of ideal precursor and the sensitivity of Cu to be oxidized, as well as the difficulties in the synthesis of small size NPs [48]. Very recently, an interesting strategy was employed in Kim's group in which two kinds of catalytic sites with different functions were combined to facilitate the CO2ER [47]. One site is the pyridinic N, acting as the CO-producing site, and the other site is the Cu NPs with the effect on promoting the reaction between *C1 or *C2 intermediates and *CO for the generation of the longer carbon product. N-doped porous carbon (Cu/NPC) materials with ca. 5 nm size Cu NPs dispersion were obtained as the cocatalyst for facilitating the generation of multi-carbon alcohols.
Herein, we report the investigation of well-dispersed nitrogen-coordinated Cu catalysts (Cu–N–CT) for CO2ER by virtue of a nitrogen-rich MOF of Cu-BTT precursor (H3BTT=1,3,5-benzenetristetrazolate). As elevating the pyrolysis temperature from 600 to 1100 °C, a slight decrease of the NPs size is observed, which lies in the range of 20–40 nm. 2. Experimental 2.1. Synthesis of Cu–BTT and the derived Cu–N–CT materials
According to the reference [49], the Cu–BTT was prepared following a modified method. CuCl2·3H2O (136.0 mg) and H3BTT (142.0 mg) were dissolved in 32.0 mL of N,N՛-dimethylformamide (DMF), and magnetically stirred for 30 min to achieve a green suspension. The solution was further transferred to a Teflon-lined autoclave
7 / 36
(100 mL) and heated at 120 °C for 12 h. After cooled down to room temperature, the as-obtained blue crystals were washed with DMF three times and then dried at 100 °C in an air atmosphere.
Synthesis of Cu–N–CT (T=600–1100 °C) materials. The blue crystals of Cu–BTT, used as the precursor, were pyrolyzed at temperatures from 600 to 1100 °C, respectively, for one hour under the Ar atmosphere. The rising-rate for heating is kept at 3 °C/min. 2.2. Material characterization
A Bruker D8 Advance X-ray diffractometer detector with Cu Kα radiation was used for the X-ray diffraction (XRD) characterization. Thermal gravimetric analyses were performed on a TG/DSC Model STA 449 F3 Netzsch instrument under argon (10 °C/min). Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and the energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) measurements were recorded on a Hitachi 4800 microscopy. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed on Holland Philips Tecnai 12 microscopy. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were measured using a Thermo Scientific ESCALAB 250Xi. N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms and pore size distribution were obtained on a Micromeritics ASAP 2020 HD88 Surface Area and Porosity Analyzer. Elemental analyses for C, H, and N were collected on a PerkinElmer 240C analyzer. The content of Cu was measured using an Inductively Coupled Plasma Emission Spectrometer (ICP-OES DV7300, USA, PerkinElmer). 2.3. Electrochemistry measurements and product analyses
Electrochemical CO2 reduction measurements were carried out on CHI 660
8 / 36
electrochemical workstation at 25 °C. For a conventional three-electrode system, a Pt sheet was used as the counter electrode. The reference electrode is Ag/AgCl. The saturated KCl aqueous solution was utilized for storing it before use. The as-synthesized Cu–N–CT was utilized as the working electrode. To prepare the catalyst ink, 30 mg sample was scattered in a mixture of 400 μL H2O+200 μL Nafion solution (mass fraction 5%)+400 μL isopropanol, followed by ultrasonic and stirring for 12 h to obtain the uniform catalyst suspension. The ink was brush coated on the carbon paper (1.0 cm × 1.0 cm) and then dried in the air (2.5 mg/cm2 loading was obtained).
A custom H-type glass cell was employed in this work, which has 160 mL volume for both sides and a cation exchange membrane of Nafion®112 for separating. Both compartments were filled with a 70.0 mL 0.1 M KHCO3 solution as the electrolyte. Before electrolysis, high purity (99.999%) of CO2 was fed into the cathode chamber for 30 min until the electrolyte was saturated (pH=6.77). Cyclic voltammetry measurements (scan rate, 50 mV/s) were performed in N2 (pH=8.73) and CO2 atmosphere, respectively. The chronopotentiometry was measured in the potential range from −1.1 to −1.8 V vs. Ag/AgCl for 2 h.
After electrolysis, the gaseous products of H2 and CO were detected by the thermal conductivity detector (TCD) in Gas Chromatography (SP-6890) using the TDX–01 column. H2 and CO standard curves are presented in Fig. S1. No hydrocarbon product was found by the flame ionization detector. The liquid product of HCOO− was quantified by the High-end ion chromatography system (940 Professional IC Vario),
9 / 36
as shown in Fig. S2. 3. Results and discussion 3.1. Synthesis and structural characterization of Cu–N–CT
The precursor for the catalyst used in this work, Cu–BTT, is isostructural with the [Cu(DMF)6][(Cu4Cl)3(BTT)8(H2O)12] created by Long et al., as evidenced in the PXRD characterization in Fig. 1(a) [49]. It has a 3D rigid framework constructed by sodalite-like cages, in which each cage is defined by eight planar BTT3− and six [Cu4Cl]7+ square-planar moieties. The whole net has a high N% content of 37.4% and a highly stable structure thanks to the contribution of the tetrazole rings. Octahedral grains with a uniform size of 100~150 nm were shown in the SEM image (Fig. 1b). A typical of type I adsorption isotherms, as shown in Fig. 1c, exhibit the microporous character of Cu–BTT with the BET of 781 m2/g and two types of micropores of 1.0 and 1.2 nm, respectively.
10 / 36
On the basis of the TG–DSC curve for Cu–BTT, we confirmed that sharp weight loss in the range of 60–350 °C is due to the release of solvents, and the decomposition of the BTT3− (Fig. 1d). The weight loss becomes gently when the temperature higher than 350 °C, and it shows no noticeable weight loss around 1000 °C. To realize the carbonization of Cu–BTT, we put the sample into the crucible under the Ar atmosphere and pyrolyze them at 600, 700, 800, 900, 1000, and 1100 °C, respectively, for 1 hour with a slow heating rate of 3 °C/min. With the release of the ligand, the derived Cu or CuO nanoparticles were embedded in the porous carbon matrix with
11 / 36
different Cu/C/N contents, which are denoted as Cu–N–C600, Cu–N–C700, Cu–N–C800, Cu–N–C900, Cu–N–C1000, and Cu–N–C1100, respectively.
12 / 36
The morphologies of the as-synthesized catalysts were examined by SEM. The original polyhedral morphology is basically maintained in Cu–N–C600 (Fig. S3a). Coral-shaped morphologies formed in Cu–N–C700 (Fig. S3b) and Cu–N–C800 (Fig. S3c) samples because of the melting, leaving lots of pores between the coral reef. As the temperature rises to 900 °C, the coral reef disappears gradually, and the uniform block particles formed in the higher temperature pyrolysis products of Cu–N–C900, Cu–N–C1000, and Cu–N–C1100 (Fig. S3d–f). The collapse of the microporous framework is evidenced in the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) and porous distribution analyses (Fig. S4a and Table S2), that is, the surface area and the micropore volume decrease a lot for each Cu–N–CT when compares with the precursor. Part of the microporous structure is maintained in the Cu–N–C600, Cu–N– C700, Cu–N–C800, and Cu–N–C900 because of the high thermal stability of Cu–BTT. According to the analysis of the BJH desorption cumulative volume, each Cu–N–CT contains rich mesoporous and macroporous distribution in the range of 30.0–100.0 nm (Fig. S4b), which is conducive to the rapid delivery of CO2, and the release of reducing products in CO2ER. Most interestingly, the total pore volume in the range of 0.85–120 nm shows a sharp decrease from 600 to 800 °C and a striking increase from 800 to 1100 °C. The highest value of 0.363 cm3/g is obtained for the Cu–N–C1100, providing plentiful porous channels for electron transfer and mass transport.
The derived Cu–N–CT has a homogeneous distribution of Cu, N, C, as revealed by the corresponding element mapping images of EDX spectroscopy (Fig. S5). The mass contents for C and N are in the ranges of 40.5–48.7, and 1.7–7.7, respectively, as
13 / 36
14 / 36
As indicated in the PXRD patterns, the carbon matrix in the Cu–N–CT materials all adopt the amorphous structure. The graphitization degree of them was verified by Raman spectroscopy. As revealed in Fig. 4, all of them show characteristic D and G bands of carbon around 1353 cm−1 and 1593 cm−1, respectively, ascribing to the disordered or defective carbon, and graphitized sp2 carbon [41–42,52]. There is an apparent correlation between the characteristic peaks in the Raman spectra and the pyrolysis temperature. The higher the carbonization temperature used, the larger the IG/ID intensity ratio we got, suggesting that the graphitization degree of carbon structure is in a high degree at higher temperatures, which is more beneficial to the electron transfer.
To reveal the oxidation state of Cu and clarify the nitrogen species in each catalyst, XPS characterization was carried out. The binding energy of C 1s (284.80 eV) is used as the reference calibration peak position in all maps. The XPS survey clearly shows
15 / 36
that the main element for each Cu–N–CT material is C, N, O, and Cu (Fig. 5a). The high-resolution Cu 2p spectra for all samples consisted of two main peaks, which are located at 932.3 eV (Cu 2p3/2) and 952.6 eV (2p1/2), respectively, indicating the metallic Cu0 chemical state (Fig. 5b) [51,53]. The characteristic peaks at 933.40 eV and the satellite-like peaks (940.80 eV and 943.60 eV) are observed in the Cu–N–C600 and Cu–N–C700 catalysts, which are convinced as the Cu2+ species [54]. Moreover, the peak at 529.2 eV is observed in the O 1s spectra of these samples (Fig. 5c), which is stemming from the lattice oxygen in CuO, also effectively confirmed the existence of CuO in the lower temperature pyrolysis products, in good agreement with the PXRD analysis result. The peak at 531.3 eV can be ascribed to the surface O or −OH adsorbed on Cu(111). The signals at 532.5 and 535.5 eV are corresponding to the physisorbed H2O and CO2, respectively, on Cu(111) [55].
16 / 36
Given that the types for the N-doped are vital for the conversion of CO2 to CO in the nitrogen-doped carbon nanotubes [56–58], the N species in Cu–N–CT catalysts were identified in detail according to the typical M–N–C materials [46,59], which is
17 / 36
divided into five groups of N, that is, pyridinic N (398.06 eV), NX–Cu/amine N (399.45 eV), pyrrolic N (400.52±0.3 eV), graphitic N or quaternary N (402.23 eV) and NO (402.23 eV), respectively (Fig. 5d). The pyridinic N, NX–Cu/amine N, and pyrrolic N are predominant in the lower temperature pyrolysis product (Tables S4– S5). However, as the elevation of the pyrolysis temperature, the unstable pyridinic N is removed a lot, which results in a significant decrease in the total N content (Fig. 6). As a result, the pyrrolic N and NX–Cu account for the main contribution to the higher temperature pyrolysis product, that is, the sum of them is 48.0% for Cu–N–C900, 57.1% Cu–N–C1000 and 61.0% for Cu–N–C1100.
To evaluate the performance of Cu–N–CT series materials towards the reduction of CO2, the cyclic voltammetry experiment in N2-/CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution from 0 to −1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl was carried out. It exhibited a dramatically improved current density and a more positive onset potential in the CO2-saturated electrolyte. An efficient CO2ER is presented when compares it to the CO2-free one (Fig. S7). To further examine the selectivity and get the product distribution of
18 / 36
CO2ER for each catalyst, the chronoamperometry tests at constant potentials from −1.1 to −1.8 V vs. Ag/AgCl were performed in CO2-saturated system at the ambient temperature and pressure (Fig. S8). The gas and liquid phase products were quantified by gas chromatography or ion chromatography. A mixed product containing CO, H2, and HCOOH is obtained in each catalyst. Previous theoretical calculations and experimental data indicated that methane formation is preferred on Cu(111) facets. Unlike the bulk Cu electrode and polycrystalline Cu reported in the literature, there are no gas products of CH4 and C2H4 detected, although the Cu (111) crystal plane is prominent in the higher pyrolysis temperature range. The low C−H selectivity could be attributed to the particle size effect of Cu NPs. Work by Rulle et al. indicated that the size of Cu NPs below to about 5 nm would cause an explosive higher catalytic current density, in which hydrogen formation is dominated [60]. Besides, the larger particles in the 5−15 nm size range generate less hydrocarbon (10%−15%) and more H2+CO (60%−70% and 20%−25%, respectively). It is generally accepted that small spherical NPs have strong CO binding, and low mobility of COad and Had, which inhibit the further surface reaction for the generation of hydrocarbons. For the Cu NPs in 20–40 nm, COad, and Had might desorb before reaction on the Cu surface. As a result, hydrocarbons are unfavored.
The current density for Cu–N–C600 is much lower as compares to that of others (Fig.
S8a). Besides, at higher potentials, the current density decreases severely, indicating the instability of it. The catalysts prepared at 700–1000 °C have a relatively high and stable current density (Fig. S8b–e). However, in consideration of the FE distribution
19 / 36
of the major products of each Cu–N–CT catalyst (Fig. S9), the high current density of Cu–N–CT (T=700–1000 °C) can be ascribed to the dominant hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). The hydrogen production efficiency of Cu–N–C600 is as high as 75% in the lower potential range of −1.1 ~ −1.4 V vs. Ag/AgCl. As the elevation of the carbonation temperature, the FE for H2 is suppressed in this potential range, which is below 40% in the Cu–N–C1100 electrode.
The visual diagrams for the product selectivity and current density in each catalyst based on CO and formic acid, respectively, are shown in Fig. 7. It is clearly observed that the product distribution relies on the carbonation temperature and the applied potential. In principle, the FE of CO and HCOOH increase as the elevation of pyrolysis temperature. However, they don't present an evident increase for the catalyst pyrolyzed from 600 to 800 °C, holding at 2.2–7.8, 2.4–12.0, 3.2–13.1, for FECO, and 1.7–20.6, 7.4–19.1, 4.1–22.0, for FEHCOOH, respectively. The Cu–N–C1100 shows the highest FE for both products. At −1.2 V vs. Ag/AgCl potential, (–0.6 V vs. RHE) 40.8% of CO (jco=0.4 mA/cm2) is obtained, behaving of 496 mV overpotential. The best FE for HCOOH is realized at −1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl (−0.9 V vs. RHE, jHCOOH=1.4 mA/cm2) of 38.1%.
20 / 36
Since CuO appears in the low-temperature pyrolyzed products, the contribution of copper oxide to the CO2ER can't be ruled out. As verified by researchers who used copper oxide electrodes directly in CO2ER, the oxides were reduced to Cu0 in situ during the process. When ultrafine CuO NPs (17 nm) was employed with different content of Nafion (1 wt%, 10 wt%, 25 wt%, 66 wt%), HCOOH was obtained as a favored product at each content, with the highest FE >60% at 25wt% [61]. The Cu(111) plane accounts for the high selectivity for HCOOH, as reported. In addition, it was reported that CuO scattered nanowires exhibit 38% FEHCOOH and 20% FECO,
21 / 36
and the reduction conversion of CuO into Cu0 happened [62]. Therefore, the presence of CuO is likely to bring out the active site of Cu0 for CO2ER.
Further elevating the carbonization temperature from 900 to 1100 °C cause lower density of Cu NPs with smaller size scattered in a carbon matrix when compares to the lower temperature pyrolyzed product (Table S4), that is, 0.67 atomic%–1.37 atomic% of Cu in 84.58 atomic%–85.4 atomic% of C with C:Cu lies in the range of 60.1–126.2 (vs. 1.99–2.68 atomic% Cu in 73.68 atomic%–79.94 atomic% C in the range of 600–800 °C; C: Cu=27.5–40.2). It means that the Cu NPs could contact with more electrolyte through the porous C thanks to the mesopores and macropores they have. The lowest Cu NPs density in Cu–N–C1100 (0.67 atomic%, C: Cu=126.2) and the highest mesoporous and microporous volume (0.363 cm3/g) guarantee the efficient penetration of the electrolyte through the carbon layers to the Cu NPs, which should account for the best performance of it.
The sufficient contact between the electrolyte and the Cu NPs is supported by the electrical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) test result when using the same electrolysis cell with each catalyst as the cathode (Fig. S10). The ohmic resistance (Rcell) exhibits a slight change of 15.4–16.6 Ω with different cathodes (Table S6). The charge transfer resistance (Rct) varies significantly when different catalysts are used. The higher temperature pyrolyzed products (900–1100 °C) exhibit higher resistance than that of the lower temperature product (700–800 °C) by 5±2 Ω, probably due to the low content of Cu in the former. However, the Cu–N–C600 exhibits a little higher resistance of 15.2 Ω, ascribing to most of the residual MOF structure it has. To verify
22 / 36
the efficient penetration of electrolytes through the carbon layers to the Cu NPs, we prepared the pyrolyzed product from the free ligand of H3BTT at 600 °C for comparison (labeled as N–C600). The outcome of N–C600 doesn't include Cu NPs in it, which exhibits much higher resistance of 466.8 Ω instead. This fact definitely proved that the higher temperature pyrolyzed Cu–N–CT could effectively decrease the resistance through the well-dispersed Cu NPs in the N-doped carbon matrix.
The CO2 capture ability also contributes to higher catalytic performance [63,64]. We carried out the corresponding experiment by using a thermogravimetric analysis apparatus, that is, 30 mg sample of each Cu–N–CT catalyst is blown repeatedly by pure N2 and CO2 flow at 303 K (Fig. S11). A weight increase of 2.3 wt%–2.6 wt% is observed in them when pure CO2 is blown. Significantly, these materials can be easily regenerated by switching the gas stream to N2. Moreover, they can withstand recyclability for 10 cycles. A stable CO2 capture signal is observed in both Cu–N– C1000 and Cu–N–C1100, of which Cu–N–C1100 has the highest weight increase of 2.6 wt% (Fig. S11f). Further increasing the pyrolyzed temperature to 1200 °C cause an increase of the FEH2 and inferior CO2 capture ability, as revealed by the co-related characterization for Cu–N–C1200 (Fig. S12, Table S7).
We also carried out the long-term chronoamperometry operation at −1.2 V and −1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl (−0.6 V and −0.9 V vs. RHE), respectively, for 10 h by using the Cu–N–C1100 catalyst (Fig. S13). The initial cathodic current density at −1.2 V remains very constant during the test period (−0.9 mA/cm2 at 10 h, vs. −1.2 mA/cm2 at 2 h). The FE for CO and HCOOH show a slight decrease of 30.0% and 21.1%, respectively,
23 / 36
when comparing it with the performance at 2 h (40.8% and 25.0%, respectively). At – 1.5 V vs. Ag/AgCl, the current density remains at 4.3 mA/cm2, and the FE for HCOOH declined to 22.2% after 10 h test because of the HER competition (Table S8).
The Tafel plots are given based on j-η data, where the overpotential η is plotted as a function of log(jco) (Fig. S14a) and log(jHCOOH) (Fig. S14b), respectively [65]. The corresponding slopes of the linear Tafel regions for Cu–N–C1000 are 278 and 300 mV/ dec, respectively.
As revealed by Peterson and nørskov, the electronic properties of catalysts have a remarkable influence on the binding energies of adsorbed intermediates in the reduction reaction, accompanying the variation of the catalytic performance, i.e., the catalogs of the reduction products, the corresponding FE and overpotential [66,67]. In contrast to the HKUST−1 oxide-derived 0D Cu/C−1000 catalyst [35], which features with atomic O modified surface structure and thereby facilitates a high alcohol FE, the higher CO2ER selectivity for Cu–N–C1100 might be attributed to the low-density dispersed Cu nanoparticles (27±2 nm), the large porous volume, the rich pyrrolic N and Cu–Nx active sites, and the stable CO2 capture ability. The uniform dispersed Cu nanoparticles through the porous carbon layers contribute to the efficient stabilization of the intermediate of COOH*, an intermediate for CO formation. It exhibits much improvement on the FE and overpotential for HCOOH than previous work on Cu/C– 1000 [35], the Cu pillar electrode made by electrodeposition [51], the Cu2O derived single crystal Cu electrode with different surfaces [68], Cu foil electrodes [69,70], and
24 / 36
Cu nanocrystals [71], etc. (Table S9).

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, a series of Cu–N–CT (T=600–1100 °C) electrocatalysts were synthesized with abundant nitrogen content and well-dispersed Cu nanoparticles in 20–40 nm sizes by carbonizing a nitrogen-rich MOF of Cu–BTT at different temperatures. These materials present significant dependence on the carbonation temperature and the applied potential. The higher temperature pyrolysis product of Cu–N–C1100, featuring the highest graphitization degree of carbon (IG/ID=1.15), the highest contribution of pyrrolic N and NX–Cu (61.0% in total), the highest mesoporous and microporous volume (0.363 cm3/g), the lowest Cu nanoparticles density in porous carbon layers (0.67 atomic%, C: Cu=126.2), and the stable CO2 capture ability (2.6 wt%), which exhibits the best catalytic activity for productions of CO (−0.6 V vs. RHE, jco=0.4 mA/cm2, ƞ=496 mV) and HCOOH (−0.9 V vs. RHE, jHCOOH=1.4 mA/cm2, ƞ=650 mV). The unusual activity may be related to the synergistic effect of low-density dispersed Cu nanoparticles (27±2 nm), the large porous volume, the rich pyrrolic N and Cu–Nx active sites, and the stable CO2 adsorption ability. Further effort will be paid for comparing the specific activities of different metal nanoparticles toward CO2ER. Declaration of Competing Interest There are no conflicts of interest to declare. sections.heading: Highlights
sections.text:
Cu–N–C electrocatalysts were prepared through the direct pyrolyze of a nitrogen-rich metal-organic framework. Well-dispersed Cu nanoparticles in 20–40 nm sizes were kept in the N-doped carbon matrix. CO (FE 40.8%) and HCOOH (FE 38.1%) were produced in high efficiencies in Cu– N–C1100 electrocatalyst. Cu–N–C1100 exhibits the highest IG/ID value, the highest contribution of pyrrolic N and NX–Cu, the highest mesoporous and microporous volume, the lowest Cu nanoparticles density in porous carbon layers, and stable CO2 capture ability.
